summary.text: A steam engine is a machine that uses steam pressure to push a piston back and forth inside a cylinder.
A connecting rod and crank turn that push into rotation, and in 1764 James Watt greatly improved the work gained per unit of fuel by condensing spent steam in a separate vessel.
By the 19th century, stationary steam engines powered the factories of the Industrial Revolution, and steam locomotives ran on the railways.

facts.value: Spent steam condensed in a separate vessel, 1764

items.prompt: A mine owner wants an engine that can feed continuous power to a machine, not just lift water. Which design was first to do this with commercial success?

options.label: Savery's steam pump, which worked directly on the water
Newcomen's atmospheric engine, which used a piston in a cylinder
Ayanz's patented pump for draining flooded mines
Hero's aeolipile, described in the first century AD

items.explain: Newcomen's engine of around 1712 was the first commercially successful engine that could transmit continuous power to a machine, improving on Savery's pump by using a piston.

items.prompt: Watt's change in 1764 got far more work from each unit of fuel. What did he do?

options.label: Moved the spent steam to a separate vessel to condense
Raised the steam pressure to push a much larger piston
Swapped the piston and cylinder for a spinning turbine
Burned the fuel inside the cylinder instead of a boiler

items.explain: Watt removed spent steam to a separate vessel for condensation, which greatly improved the work obtained per unit of fuel.

items.prompt: Mill machinery must spin, but a piston only moves back and forth in a straight line. What turns one motion into the other?

options.label: A boiler fitted around the outside of the cylinder
A condenser that cools the steam after each stroke
A connecting rod and crank attached to the piston
A governor that cools the steam between strokes

items.explain: The pushing force can be transformed by a connecting rod and crank into rotational force for work.

items.prompt: A visitor asks whether the burning gases from the fire flow into the cylinder and shove the piston. What is the right answer?

options.label: Yes, the burning gases push the piston directly
Yes, but only in engines built for locomotives
No, because the engine runs on stored heat rather than fire
No, the steam doing the work is kept apart from the combustion products

items.explain: Steam engines are external combustion engines, so the working fluid is separated from the combustion products.

items.prompt: A mine owner wants a much larger version of Savery's steam pump. What problems should he expect?

options.label: It would use far more fuel than Newcomen's engine
It would lift water only a short way and risk a boiler explosion
It could not work at all without a flywheel and crankshaft
It would need a person at hand to drive each stroke

items.explain: Small Savery engines were effective, but larger ones had a very limited lift height and were prone to boiler explosions.

items.prompt: Power stations moved from piston steam engines to steam turbines. What was the reason?

options.label: Turbines cost less, ran at higher speed and were more efficient
Small turbines were far more efficient than piston engines
Piston steam engines were no longer made anywhere in the world
Turbines were easier to build in small sizes for home use

items.explain: Steam turbines replaced reciprocating engines in power generation due to lower cost, higher operating speed and higher efficiency; small turbines are much less efficient than large ones.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A steam engine is a heat engine that does mechanical work using steam as its working fluid. Steam pressure pushes a piston back and forth inside a cylinder. A connecting rod and crank then turn that back-and-forth push into turning force that can do work. It is an external combustion engine, which means the steam doing the work is kept apart from the products of the fire.

paragraphs.heading: Early experiments
paragraphs.text: People toyed with steam long before it did useful work. In the first century AD, Hero of Alexandria, an engineer in Roman Egypt, described the aeolipile, a simple steam-driven device. For centuries afterward the few steam engines known were mostly experiments to show off what steam could do. In 1606 the Spanish inventor Jerónimo de Ayanz received patents for 50 steam inventions, among them a pump for draining flooded mines, and in 1690 Denis Papin first used a piston to lift weights.

paragraphs.heading: Savery and Newcomen
paragraphs.text: The first commercial steam device was Thomas Savery's water pump of 1698. Condensing steam made a vacuum that drew water up, and steam pressure then pushed it higher. It was cheap, but it could lift water only a short way and its boilers tended to explode. Around 1712 Thomas Newcomen built the atmospheric engine, the first commercially successful engine able to give continuous power to a machine. It worked by condensing steam under a piston to make a partial vacuum, and though inefficient it drained mines deeper than older methods could.

paragraphs.heading: Watt and turning motion
paragraphs.text: In 1764 James Watt made a crucial change: he moved the spent steam into a separate vessel to condense, which greatly raised the work gained from each unit of fuel. In 1780 James Pickard patented a flywheel and crankshaft that drew turning motion from an improved Newcomen engine.

paragraphs.heading: Powering an age
paragraphs.text: By the 19th century, stationary steam engines ran the factories of the Industrial Revolution. Paddle steamers took the place of sailing ships, and steam locomotives worked the railways. Piston steam engines stayed the main source of power until the early 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Giving way
paragraphs.text: Better electric motors and internal combustion engines gradually pushed steam engines out of commercial use. In power generation, steam turbines replaced piston engines because they cost less, ran faster and were more efficient. Even so, as of October 2026, large piston steam engines are still being built in Germany.
